title: Smallest Sufficient Team
statement:
You get `req_skills`, a list of distinct skills a project needs, and `people`, where `people[i]` is the list of distinct skills that person `i` has (each of them also appears in `req_skills`). A team, written as a list of person indices, is *sufficient* when every skill in `req_skills` is held by at least one of its members.

Return the indices of a sufficient team with the fewest possible people. If several smallest teams exist, any one of them is accepted, and the indices may be listed in any order. At least one sufficient team always exists.
constraints: req_skills[i] contains only lowercase English letters
The strings in req_skills are distinct
people[i][j] contains only lowercase English letters
The strings in each people[i] are distinct
Every skill in people[i] appears in req_skills
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every group of people means up to 2^60 subsets. The skills, however, number at most 16, so any set of covered skills fits in a 16-bit mask and there are at most 65,536 such sets. Instead of asking "which people?", ask "what is the fewest people needed to cover exactly this set of skills?" for every mask, and remember the last person added so the team can be rebuilt.

## Approach

1. Give each skill a bit via `skillIndex`; `full` has every bit set.
2. Turn each person's skill list into a mask in `masks`.
3. `size[mask]` is the fewest people whose skills together form `mask`; start with `size[0] = 0` and everything else `Infinity`.
4. Visit masks in increasing order. From a reachable `mask`, adding `person` reaches `next = mask | masks[person]`; if that uses fewer people than known, store the new `size`, the `lastPerson` and the `previous` mask. A superset is never smaller numerically, so every mask is final before it is visited.
5. Starting from `full`, follow `previous` back to `0`, collecting `lastPerson` along the way into `team`.

## Example 1, step by step

`java`, `nodejs`, `reactjs` get bits 1, 2 and 4, so `masks = [1, 2, 6]` and `full = 7`. From mask 0, each person alone reaches 1, 2 and 6 with size 1. From mask 1, person 1 reaches 3 and person 2 reaches 7, both with size 2; later masks find nothing smaller. Walking back: mask 7 came from person 2 and mask 1, and mask 1 came from person 0 and mask 0. The team is `[2, 0]`, the same team as `[0, 2]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(2^m · n) for m skills and n people: each mask tries every person, at most 65,536 · 60 steps.
- Space: O(2^m) for `size`, `lastPerson` and `previous`.

## Pitfalls

- Greedily taking the person with the most new skills can be wrong (Test 5 shows a case).
- Store how each mask was reached; recomputing the team from sizes alone is awkward.
- People with no skills, or skills someone else already covers, must not be added; the strict `<` comparison prevents that.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `skillIndex` | skill name to its bit position |
| `full` | mask with every required skill |
| `masks` | each person's skills as a mask |
| `size` | fewest people forming each mask |
| `lastPerson`, `previous` | the person added to reach a mask, and the mask before it |
| `team` | the rebuilt list of chosen indices |
